title: Tenant onramp: egress probes and split-DNS playbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for tenant onramp patterns we discussed during the 2024-11-06 workshop. Focus: egress control, DNS handoff, and detection/probing strategies to ensure correct routing for private deployments (VPC, VPC-peering, and transit models).

Audience and constraints:
- Solutions engineering + customer networking teams.
- Customers may be in AWS, GCP, or Azure; primary target in AWS for initial POC.
- Customer networks are typically: single VPC (dev), multiple VPCs per-svc (prod), or corporate networks with transit hubs.
- Compliance constraints: no internet egress for PHI workloads unless through approved proxy; audit logs required.

Summary (top-level recommendation):
1) Default: use conditional split-DNS + interface VPC endpoints for AWS services + an egress edge proxy (TLS passthrough or MITM where permitted) for controlled internet access.
2) For customers that cannot run an edge proxy: use a tightly scoped NAT gateway in a dedicated egress VPC with explicit route tables and monitoring.
3) Prefer private hosted zones with conditional forwarding to customer DNS resolvers for zone handoff; avoid editing customer authoritative zone records.

Architectures considered (short):
A. Direct VPC Peering to Redwood private subnets
   - Pros: low latency, simple routing for private endpoints
   - Cons: Not transitive; many peering relationships if multiple customers; limited DNS flexibility (need resolver rules)

B. Transit VPC / Transit Gateway (TGW) hub-and-spoke
   - Pros: Scales for many customers, centralizes egress/proxy, supports route propagation
   - Cons: More ops overhead; shared egress introduces blast radius if misconfigured

C. On-prem/Customer VPN with DNS conditional forward + interface endpoints
   - Pros: Customer retains DNS and egress control; fits highly regulated customers
   - Cons: Complexity on customer side; latency and bandwidth limits on VPNs

D. Private Link / Interface Endpoints into Redwood-managed VPCs
   - Pros: Uses endpoint services, no routing changes in customer VPCs; well-suited for hosted API model
   - Cons: Limitations on multitenancy features (need separate endpoint services or permissions); more AWS account-level configuration for customers

DNS options and tradeoffs:
1) Split-horizon (private hosted zone in customer account; resolver rules point to Redwood DNS for service records):
   - Best when customer wants control and can host zone. Allows customer to keep public records unchanged.
   - Requires: Private hosted zone present in customer VPC, or conditional forwarder rules to Redwood resolver IPs.

2) Conditional forwarding to customer resolver (Route 53 Resolver rules or dnsmasq on proxy):
   - Good compromise: Redwood resolves service records only for our subdomain and forwards others to customer.
   - Watch out for cycles and TTL discrepancies.

3) Centralized DNS in Redwood with delegation (rare):
   - Redwood hosts service subdomain and customer adds delegation at their parent domain. Works for customers willing to delegate.

DNS pitfalls we've hit in prior POCs:
- Customer firewalls blocking outbound UDP DNS (53) — causes long timeouts and fallback to TCP, breaking some clients.
- Resolver caching mismatch when switching takeover strategies (endless 301/302 from cached endpoints).
- CNAME chains across split-horizon leading to incorrect public endpoints being returned.

Egress control options and recommendations:
- Use egress probes (heartbeat) from customer VPC to validate:
  1) Internal-only access to Redwood endpoints through VPC peering/TGW
  2) Internet-bound access via customer-managed proxy or Redwood edge (when allowed)
- Probe plan: two kinds of probes (connectivity and behavior):
  - Connectivity probe: small TCP/HTTPS handshake to a known Redwood test path (200 OK expected). Runs every 30s from each AZ subnet used.
  - Behavior probe: fetch a small JSON which contains declared-source metadata (e.g., "via_proxy":true) to confirm inspection/preserved headers. Runs every 5 min.
- Failure modes and automated responses:
  - Transient failures (>=3 consecutive failures across >=2 subnets in 10 min): raise PagerDuty and cutover to fallback (if configured)
  - Persistent failures: trigger rollback (remove custom route, move to NAT egress, or open a support case)

Proxy vs NAT decision matrix:
- If customer requires header preservation, mutual TLS, or fine-grained auth -> edge proxy (layer 7)
- If customer disallows L7 interception -> NAT + IP allowlist (simpler but less observable)
- For regulated workloads (HIPAA/PAY): insist on customer-manged egress through approved NGFW or Redwood-managed dedicated egress in customer account via an Egress VPC (preferred).

VPC endpoints (AWS) guidance:
- Gateway endpoints (S3/Dynamo): create in each customer subnet used by the onramp services; document bucket ARNs and policy templates.
- Interface endpoints: expose required Redwood API endpoints as endpoint services where possible. Use security group templates that require least privilege (source = customer subnet SGs or CIDRs).
- Endpoint policy templates: provide 2 sample policies: minimal read-only and full-call (for admin flows).

Operational checklist (POC runbook):
- Pre-work (owned by SE and Customer NetEng):
  1) Confirm account IDs, VPC IDs, and CIDR ranges.
  2) Share diagram with CIDRs and proposed route table entries.
  3) Agree on DNS handoff method (private zone vs resolver rules vs delegation).
  4) Determine egress model (proxy, NAT, Redwood-managed egress).
  5) Decide monitoring endpoints and PagerDuty recipients.

- Deployment steps (day-0 to day-3):
  Day 0: create role-based access for Redwood SE, spin up test subnets and security groups
  Day 1: deploy VPC peering / TGW attachments, create resolver rules and private hosted zones
  Day 2: provision interface endpoints and attach endpoint services (if chosen). Deploy egress proxy in egress VPC (if chosen)
  Day 3: run egress/connectivity probes; smoke test with sample API calls; validate DNS resolution in all AZs/subnets

- Validation tests (automated):
  - DNS: resolve redwood-service.<customer-subdomain> from an instance in each subnet; assert answer is private IP and correct TTL
  - Connectivity: run 100 small requests (20ms-200ms expectation) and check success ratio >=99%
  - Headers: verify client IP preservation or proxy headers depending on model
  - Cost sanity: estimate NAT/egress charges for 100K tokens/day sample (provide ballpark numbers in onboarding)

Logging, tracing and auditability:
- Require VPC Flow Logs (at least for the duration of the POC) to be enabled to an S3 bucket or CloudWatch with 90-day retention.
- App-level traces should include route metadata ("via": "peering|tgw|egress-proxy") for debugging.
- Provide a sample Kibana/CloudWatch dashboard for quick health checks (probe pass rate, DNS failures, error codes).

Security considerations and red-team notes:
- Avoid storing private keys on proxies without HSM/KMS integration.
- If MITM TLS is needed, document consent and ensure key rotation policies are in place.
- Make sure SG rules do not open 0.0.0.0/0 where not required — prefer sg-to-sg references.

Rollout strategy and rollback playbook:
- Canary: choose 1–2 non-critical subnets and route 5–10% of traffic through the new path; monitor for 1–2 hours.
- Gradual increase: 10% -> 50% -> 100% with min 30–60 min observation windows.
- Automatic rollback triggers: probe failure threshold, increase in 5xx > 3x baseline, or DNS resolution mismatches.

Unresolved questions / customer decisions needed: (to capture in handoff doc)
- Does the customer have an existing TLS intercepting proxy? If yes, what headers survive interception?
- Can the customer create private hosted zones and resolver rules in their account? (important for split-DNS)
- Is there an approved NGFW vendor we need to integrate with for egress (e.g., Palo Alto, Zscaler)?
- Are there IP allowlist windows we need for internal ops (support team) prior to full handoff?

Action items (owners & ETA):
- Aisha: produce security group / endpoint policy templates (ETA 2024-11-13)
- Miguel: Terraform module draft for egress VPC + proxy (ETA 2024-11-20)
- Samir: automated probe code and CloudWatch dashboards (ETA 2024-11-15)
- Becky: customer-facing diagram + onboarding checklist (ETA 2024-11-10)

Appendix: quick troubleshooting commands (AWS-focused)
- Test DNS: dig @<resolver-ip> redwood-service.customer.internal +short +tcp
- Check resolver rules: aws route53resolver list-resolver-rules --creator-request-id "customer-onramp"
- VPC peering: aws ec2 describe-vpc-peering-connections --filters Name=requester-vpc-info.cidr-block,Values=<cidr>
- Endpoint status: aws ec2 describe-vpc-endpoints --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=<vpc>

Notes to self / workshop fragments (raw):
- Customer B had intermittent DNS failures due to UDP blackhole — recommend TCP fallback tests during POC.
- Consider tiny TTL (30s) during canary so we can flip quickly if needed.
- For BYO-network customers, create an onboarding template with 1) CIDR diagram, 2) resolver rules snippet, 3) SG templates, 4) endpoint policy examples.

If this doc looks good, next step is to convert the checklist into a Terraform + docs bundle and attach to the GitHub repo (linked above).

-- end of draft playbook --
